analysis.one_liner: Creates universal government-funded health coverage with no deductibles or copays, financed by taxes on corporations and high earners.
analysis.headline: The single-payer bill drew 92 cosponsors and held two subcommittee hearings, but never received a committee vote or a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have replaced Medicare, Medicaid, federal employee coverage, military health coverage, and most private insurance with a single publicly funded system run by the states under federal rules. Every U.S. resident would be enrolled automatically and issued a health card covering hospital care, doctors, prescription drugs, dental, mental health, substance abuse treatment, and long-term care — with no deductibles, coinsurance, or copayments for acute care and no balance billing. It would have been paid for by raising individual and corporate income tax rates, adding a surtax on incomes over $1 million, increasing the hospital insurance payroll tax, and repealing tax breaks for oil and gas drilling, securities dealers, and real estate exchanges.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident would gain guaranteed coverage with no out-of-pocket costs for acute care, portable across state lines, regardless of employment, income, or health status. The roughly 39 million uninsured Americans at the time, people denied coverage for pre-existing conditions, Medicare patients facing cost-sharing, and families paying premiums would all be enrolled automatically. Community health centers and underserved areas would get dedicated funding, and patients could see any qualified provider without a network.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The uninsured and everyone with health costs

how_it_helps.text: Every U.S. citizen, national, and lawful resident alien would be entitled to coverage under a state health security program, enrolled automatically at birth or upon acquiring lawful status, with a health security card and benefits portable between states.

Coverage would include hospital care, practitioner services, preventive care, prescription drugs, dental, mental health, substance abuse treatment, long-term care, and more — and would charge no deductibles, coinsurance, or copayments for acute care, with providers barred from charging patients anything beyond the program payment.

The bill would supersede Medicare, Medicaid, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, and CHAMPUS after December 31, 1994, replacing five separate systems with one card, while preserving veterans' and Indian Health Service benefits.
The federal Board would negotiate maximum prices with drug manufacturers and pay pharmacies from an approved-drug list, directly attacking drug prices rather than subsidizing them.

It would fund primary care training, community health centers, maternal and child health grants, and payment incentives for medically underserved urban and rural areas, and would finance roughly 81 to 91 percent of each state's program costs from the federal trust fund.

analysis.who_pays: The financing falls on high-income households and corporations: increased individual and corporate income tax rates with a health security premium, a new surtax on incomes over $1 million, a higher hospital insurance (Medicare) payroll tax extended to state and local employees, permanent limits on itemized deductions and personal exemptions for high earners, permanent top estate and gift tax rates, a monthly long-term care premium for non-low-income elderly, and repeal of tax preferences for oil and gas drilling, real estate like-kind exchanges, securities dealers' accounting, and certain advertising and foreign-corporation tax rules. Employers would trade insurance premiums for a payroll tax increase.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners, corporations, and drug makers

drawbacks.text: The financing was a large, broad tax increase: higher individual and corporate income tax rates, a surtax on incomes over $1 million, a bigger hospital insurance payroll tax that would have hit state and local government workers for the first time, and a monthly long-term care premium on elderly people who are not low-income.

Hospital operating costs would have been capped by annual global budgets, and the national health budget could not grow faster than the economy (GDP) — supporters called this cost control; skeptics warned it could mean rationing by budget rather than by price.

Drug coverage would be limited to a Board-approved formulary at Board-negotiated maximum prices, and services covered by national practice guidelines could be excluded if not delivered according to those guidelines — meaning a federal board, not your doctor alone, would define what is covered.
The bill banned the sale of any private insurance that duplicates program benefits, so people who wanted to buy supplemental private coverage on top of the public plan could not.

Mental health and substance abuse treatment beyond 20 outpatient visits or 15 inpatient days per year would be subject to utilization review, and the Board could limit how often eyeglasses, hearing aids, and durable equipment are replaced.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was the most complete universal-coverage proposal of its era: every resident covered, zero cost-sharing, an end to balance billing and pre-existing-condition denials, and financing drawn progressively from millionaires, corporations, and tax preferences rather than from premiums and deductibles. The costs were equally real — a large tax increase, hospital budgets capped at GDP-plus growth, a federal formulary for drugs, and the elimination of duplicate private insurance. Whether global budgets would have produced lower prices or waiting lists was never tested, because the bill never even reached a committee vote. The honest reading is that the policy trade-offs were debatable, but the process failure was not: with 92 cosponsors and two hearings, no committee ever voted, so the public never got to see the argument settled on the merits.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in five House committees and their subcommittees for nearly two years; the only formal action beyond referral was two subcommittee hearings in February 1994, and Congress ended in January 1995 without any vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim McDermott, a physician, introduced the bill on March 3, 1993 with 52 original cosponsors, and it was referred jointly to five committees: Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Armed Services, Post Office and Civil Service, and Veterans' Affairs.

Within six weeks the bill was divided among at least six subcommittees, including Social Security, Health, Compensation and Employee Benefits, Hospitals and Health Care, and Health and the Environment — a referral pattern that meant no single committee owned the bill.

On August 10, 1993, the House action list cross-referenced H.R. 2264, the Democratic leadership's competing managed-competition health bill, signaling that the House's attention had moved to the administration-backed approach.

Two subcommittee hearings were held in February 1994, and McDermott gave repeated floor statements through mid-1994, but the record shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers and pharmaceutical manufacturers kept the existing employer-based insurance system intact — the bill would have ended duplicate private coverage and imposed negotiated drug price maximums. The Democratic leadership's own plan also failed, so the pre-reform status quo of private insurance, Medicare, and Medicaid continued until the Affordable Care Act in 2010.

for.name: Jim McDermott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, recruited 52 original cosponsors, and gave repeated floor statements defending it through June 1994.

for.name: 92 House cosponsors (91 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.role: Cosponsors, about one-fifth of the House
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including liberal Democrats such as Conyers, Pelosi, Stark, Waxman, Rangel, and Schumer, and Independent Bernie Sanders.

for.name: House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce subcommittees
for.what_they_did: Held hearings on the bill in February 1994, the only formal consideration it received.

against.name: Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chairman, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on H.R. 1200; the committee with primary jurisdiction devoted its health care effort to the Clinton administration's competing bill.

against.name: President Bill Clinton
against.what_they_did: Advanced his own Health Security Act (managed competition with employer mandates) rather than endorsing single payer, so the majority party's institutional energy went to a rival bill.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.role: Industry lobby (e.g., Health Insurance Association of America's 'Harry and Louise' campaign)
against.what_they_did: Ran a nationwide advertising and lobbying campaign against government-run health insurance during 1993-1994.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: Lobbied and advertised against price controls and formularies in the 1993-1994 health care debate.

sides.party_line_note: All 92 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's sole Independent, Bernie Sanders; no Republican sponsored the bill, and the Democratic leadership pursued its own competing plan instead.

industries.note: The bill banned the sale of any insurance duplicating program benefits and replaced Medicare, Medicaid, FEHBP, and CHAMPUS — eliminating the private major-medical insurance market entirely. Its survival depended on this bill never advancing.

A federal Board would negotiate maximum prices with manufacturers and pay only for an approved-drug list, ending the industry's ability to set U.S. prices without a negotiating counterparty. U.S. patients currently pay among the highest drug prices in the world in part because no such negotiation exists.

Hospitals would gain guaranteed payment for every patient and an end to uncompensated care, but would operate under annual global budgets that could not grow faster than GDP, and providers would be barred from charging patients beyond the program payment.

Doctors would be paid on a negotiated fee-for-service schedule with guaranteed reimbursement within 60 days, but would face mandatory assignment (program payment as full payment), an expanded ban on self-referrals, and practice-pattern profiling with sanctions for outliers.
The bill repealed the intangible drilling cost deduction and percentage depletion for oil and gas wells to help fund coverage — a long-standing industry tax preference.
Employers would pay a higher hospital insurance tax but would stop paying health insurance premiums for workers, ending their role as the gatekeepers of American health coverage.
